title: The soul as a bride
hook: many hymns speak as a bride longing for her Husband Lord, a picture of the soul's love

segments.voice: Yesterday, sahaj, the ease that comes when the grip lets go; your line was ease. Today, the Granth's warmest picture of the soul.

The Gurus were all men. Yet again and again in the Guru Granth Sahib, they sing in a woman's voice. A young bride at the window, getting ready, wondering if her beloved will come, asking her friends how they won his love. Guru Nanak does it. Guru Arjan does it. Bhagat Kabir, whose hymns sit beside theirs, does it too. Why that voice, of all voices, to speak about God? Today's word opens it: suhagan.
screen: `THE GURUS WERE MEN.` → `THEY SING AS A BRIDE.` → `WHY THAT VOICE?`

segments.voice: Suhagan means the happily married bride, the one united with her husband. Her opposite in the hymns is duhagan, the bride left alone, forgotten. In this picture, God is the Husband, the Beloved, and every soul is the bride, whether the person singing is a man or a woman. It's not a statement about men and women. It's a picture of love. In the hymns' picture, the bride can't win love by arguing or bargaining. She can get ready, keep faith, and wait. So how does a bride become suhagan? Not through jewelry or fancy clothes, the hymns say, but through humility, sweet speech and love. In one of Guru Nanak's hymns in Tilang, the bride is told to go and ask the happy wives how they won the Husband. The answer, roughly: accept whatever he does as good, drop your own cleverness and your own commands, and do as he says. That's hukam, the order, turned into romance. The picture comes closest to home at a Sikh wedding. The Laavan, four verses by Guru Ram Das, are sung while the couple walk around the Guru Granth Sahib. They're a wedding song, and also about the soul's marriage to God, stage by stage. So every Sikh wedding is two weddings at once. And the picture says something tender: in these hymns, what lies between a person and God isn't fear or duty. It's longing, and belonging.
screen: `SUHAGAN — THE UNITED BRIDE.` · `EVERY SOUL IS THE BRIDE.` · `NOT JEWELS — HUMILITY AND LOVE.` · `THE LAAVAN: TWO WEDDINGS AT ONCE.` · then, large: `THE SOUL IS A BRIDE.`

segments.voice: On paper or in your phone, write one honest line of longing in your own words, for God if that's your language, or for peace, for someone you miss, for the person you hope to become: I wish, I miss, I'm waiting for. Read it once, quietly. Then set it down and sit with the feeling it leaves, without fixing it.
Suhagan. The bride united with her beloved. In the Granth, a picture of the soul, any soul, joined with God through love and humility.
Your line: the soul is a bride. The one at the window is still in the love story. That's day two hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: At a Sikh wedding, the Anand Karaj, the four verses of the Laavan by Guru Ram Das are read and sung as the couple walk around the Guru Granth Sahib, and they're understood as describing both the marriage and the soul's union with God.

fork.setup: you're the bride in Guru Nanak's hymn, asking the happy wives how they won his love. what do they tell you?
options: give up your pride, and let him have his way.
fork.reveal: accept what he does as good and drop your own cleverness: humility and surrender to his will, hukam told as a love story.

original.note: Gurmukhi: suhagan, the happily married bride; from suhag, the good fortune of a married woman.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bride is just a wedding picture.
what it means: in the Granth, every soul is a bride, and union with God comes through love and humility, not ornaments or argument.
what a scholar hears: suhagan and duhagan, from suhag, marital good fortune; a devotional convention shared with Sufi and bhakti poetry, where the male poet takes the woman's voice.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): Kabir no longer counted among the Gurus (hook and myth); cut the stock 'surprises people' opener and the unsourced picture of brides in old Punjab; Tilang paraphrase tightened to the hymn (accept what he does as good, drop cleverness and one's own command); 'reaches its height' and 'the deepest thing' softened.

The hymn where the bride asks the happy wives how they won the Husband (jaae puchhahu sohaaganee) is attributed to Guru Nanak in Tilang, around Ang 722; confirm the Ang and the paraphrase ('give up your pride, let him have his way').
Laavan cited as Suhi Mahala 4, Ang 773–774; confirm.
The note that the bridal voice is a convention shared with Sufi and bhakti poetry is stated as a scholarly observation, without ranking; confirm wording.
Suhagan etymology from suhag (marital good fortune) is standard; confirm spelling ਸੁਹਾਗਣਿ as used in Gurbani.
